Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to plot a function on a graphing calculator and then use our plot to find accurate approximations of the function's roots.

Content:
This lesson is designed to help prepare you for the parts of the AP Calculus exam where graphing calculators are needed.

Content:
If you want to succeed on the AP Calculus exam, then you must acquire a physical graphing calculator and use it when completing this lesson.

Content:
Do not use any other type of online tool, as you will not be allowed to use it during the exam. You need to practice with the specific calculator that you will use on the AP exam so that you can solve problems quickly without wasting any time troubleshooting your calculator.

Content:
A comprehensive list of calculators that are permitted in the AP Calculus exams can be found here.

Content:
Throughout this lesson, we will list buttons that feature on a TI-84 Plus CE-T graphing calculator.

Content:
Similar models will have the same or similar buttons, and even dissimilar models may have similar buttons.

Content:
If you have a different calculator model and cannot find the right buttons to press, the best way to resolve this is to either to

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] (a) consult your calculator's manual, or

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] (b) search online for a video that explains how to operate your calculator.

Content:
The best way to get familiar with your calculator is to consult its manual. Manuals can usually be found online. For example, a link to the manual for a TI-84 Plus CE-T can be found by entering the following query into a search engine.

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] online manual TI-84 Plus CE-T

Content:
If you have a different model calculator, replace "TI-84 Plus CE-T" in the query above with your calculator's model.

Content:
Answers to common questions can be found by searching for online videos explaining how the calculator works. For example, to find a video that shows how to plot a function on a TI-84, you might type the following query into a search engine.

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] video plot a function on a TI-84 graphing calculator

Content:
Again, replace "TI-84" in the query above with your calculator's model. Also, bear in mind that videos for similar models might also help.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to plot a function on a graphing calculator and then use our plot to find accurate approximations of the function's roots.

Content:
This lesson is designed to help prepare you for the parts of the AP Calculus exam where graphing calculators are needed.

Content:
If you want to succeed on the AP Calculus exam, then you must acquire a physical graphing calculator and use it when completing this lesson.

Content:
Do not use any other type of online tool, as you will not be allowed to use it during the exam. You need to practice with the specific calculator that you will use on the AP exam so that you can solve problems quickly without wasting any time troubleshooting your calculator.

Content:
A comprehensive list of calculators that are permitted in the AP Calculus exams can be found here.

Content:
Throughout this lesson, we will list buttons that feature on a TI-84 Plus CE-T graphing calculator.

Content:
Similar models will have the same or similar buttons, and even dissimilar models may have similar buttons.

Content:
If you have a different calculator model and cannot find the right buttons to press, the best way to resolve this is to either to

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] (a) consult your calculator's manual, or

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] (b) search online for a video that explains how to operate your calculator.

Content:
The best way to get familiar with your calculator is to consult its manual. Manuals can usually be found online. For example, a link to the manual for a TI-84 Plus CE-T can be found by entering the following query into a search engine.

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] online manual TI-84 Plus CE-T

Content:
If you have a different model calculator, replace "TI-84 Plus CE-T" in the query above with your calculator's model.

Content:
Answers to common questions can be found by searching for online videos explaining how the calculator works. For example, to find a video that shows how to plot a function on a TI-84, you might type the following query into a search engine.

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] video plot a function on a TI-84 graphing calculator

Content:
Again, replace "TI-84" in the query above with your calculator's model. Also, bear in mind that videos for similar models might also help.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Plotting a Function

Content:
So, our goal is to plot some functions on a graphing calculator and then use these to approximate the function's roots.

Content:
Let's start by plotting the following function:

Content:
[MATH: f(x)=x^3-\sin x.]

Content:
Watch Out! Since [MATH: f(x)] involves a trigonometric function, we must put our calculator into radians mode!

Content:
To plot the function, we first press the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,y=\,}] button, and then enter the function definition in the first available space (usually labeled [MATH: Y_1=]) using the following sequence of buttons:

Content:
[MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}X,T,\theta,n}\qquad
\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\land\,} \qquad
\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,3\,} \qquad
\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\blacktriangleright\,} \qquad
\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,-\,} \qquad
\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\sin\,} \qquad
\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}X,T,\theta,n}\qquad
\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,)\,}]

Content:
We then press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{graph}\,}] to graph the function.

Content:
To get a better view of our function, we can adjust the window settings using the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{window}\,}] button. Press this button, and then enter the following settings:

Content:
[MATH: Xmin|= − 2; Xmax|= 2; Ymin|= − 3; Ymax|= 3]

Content:
Remember to use the negative [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,(-)\,}] button when entering the negative numbers.

Content:
Once you've entered these settings, press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{graph}\,}] once more. Your calculator should then draw the following graph:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6200fb5b748af7003c4e4e299fbdfa9c]

Content:
Notice that the [MATH: x] and [MATH: y]-axes have been restricted as follows:

Content:
- For the horizontal axis, we have [MATH: x \in [-2,2].]
- For the vertical axis, we have [MATH: y \in [-3,3].]

Content:
Make sure you can replicate this graph on your graphing calculator before continuing. This includes adjusting the window settings, which will become important later in the lesson.

---

Item 3 — Tutorial: Finding the Root of a Function

Content:
So, we have the function [MATH: f(x),] defined as

Content:
[MATH: f(x)=x^3-\sin x.]

Content:
Our plot of this function is shown again below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/609d031ed09f9de730c2d681504c2e23]

Content:
The graph shows that the positive root of this function lies inside the interval [MATH: x \in [0,2].] Our goal now is to find an accurate approximation for this root using our graphing calculator's [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{zero}\,}] command.

Content:
To access the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{zero}\,}] command, we first make sure that our function [MATH: f(x)] is plotted, and the root we want to find is clearly in view. Then, we press the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{2nd}\,}] button followed by [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{calc}\,}.] We then select [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{zero}\,}] from the menu, followed by [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{enter}\,}.]

Content:
The calculator will now ask us to specify an interval containing the root and an initial guess. First, we select a "left bound," followed by a "right bound," followed by our "guess." To specify these values, we use the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\blacktriangleleft\,}] and [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\blacktriangleright\,}] buttons to move the cursor along the curve, and press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\textrm{enter}\,}] to select.

Content:
In this particular case, we enter the following when prompted:

Content:
- The "left bound" should be a value close to the root on its left-hand side. Let's pick [MATH: 0.]
- The "right bound" should be a value close to the root on its right-hand side. Let's pick [MATH: 1.5.]
- The "guess" could be any number from the interval [MATH: x\in [0,1.5].] Let's pick [MATH: 0.5.]

Content:
Our interval and guess are highlighted below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c4b1546202bdaaa35f0e3416929f3633]

Content:
At the bottom of the display, the calculator will return the following value for the zero (i.e., the root):

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: x = 0.928\,626\,3]

Content:
And that's it! We've successfully used the calculator's root-finding functions to approximate the positive root of [MATH: f(x)] to seven decimal places.

---

Content:
Suppose we want to find the smallest positive root of the following function:

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x\sqrt x} + 24\cos\left(\dfrac{x+1}{48}\right)]

Content:

Content:

Then, we press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\textrm{enter}}] followed by [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\textrm{enter}}] once more.

Content:

Content:

Content:

Item 12 — Example: Approximating a Root of a Function: Roots Outside the Standard Range

Example Prompt:
Find an approximation for the root of the function

[MATH: f(x) = \sin\left(\dfrac{\sqrt x}{10}\right).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we plot [MATH: y=f(x)] using a graphing calculator to find an interval that contains the root. Since [MATH: f(x)] contains trigonometric functions, we need to make sure that the calculator is in [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{RAD}\,}] (radians) mode.

To plot the function, we press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,y=\,}] and enter the function definition in the first available space. We then press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{graph}\,}] to graph the function.

The default view on most graphing calculators is [MATH: x \in [-10,10], y \in [-10,10].] However, in this instance, the root falls outside the default view.

To get a better view, we might need to either

- zoom in or out, or
- adjust the window ranges.

We can adjust the window settings using the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{window}\,}] button (or equivalent).

In our case, the appropriate window ranges could be the following:

- for the horizontal axis, [MATH: x \in [850,1\,200]]
- for the vertical axis, [MATH: y \in [-1,1]]

[IMG: /graphics/932219effe665fc94bc1a4b66a3c0bfb]

The graph shows that the smallest root lies inside the interval [MATH: x\in [900, 1100].]

To get a good approximation for the root, we use the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{zero}\,}] command (or equivalent). This is usually accessed by pressing the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{calc}\,}] button (or equivalent). Note that we sometimes need to press the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{2nd}\,}] or [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{shift}\,}] button first.

We enter the following when prompted:

- The "left bound" should be a value close to the root on its left-hand side. Let's pick [MATH: 900.]
- The "right bound" should be a value close to the root on its right-hand side. Let's pick [MATH: 1\,100.]
- The "guess" could be any number from [MATH: [900,1\,100].] Let's pick [MATH: 1\,000.]

[IMG: /graphics/bc69eb764ddf53d57e4ece343ad4a7ff]

The calculator returns the zero

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: x \approx 986.960\,44.]

Rounding to [MATH: 2] decimal places, we obtain the following:

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: x \approx 986.96]
